newsitem.title: USA: Leaf rust seen cutting Oklahoma wheat yields.
newsitem.headline: Leaf rust seen cutting Oklahoma wheat yields.

text.p: A significant outbreak of leaf rust fungus in Oklahoma's wheat crop may cut yields on susceptible plants by 10 to 15 percent, plant pathologists said Tuesday.
The epidemic comes at a time when many plants are trying to shake off the damaging effects of a mid-April freeze.
"The wheat's trying to recover from the freeze and now it's getting zapped by the rust," said Gene Krenzer, small grains specialist at Oklahoma State University in Stillwater, Okla.
"It's very significant right now in the southwest part of the state and we're expecting it to be a major problem across the state in coming weeks," Krenzer said.

He estimated that one-third to one-half of Oklahoma's wheat acreage had been planted to varieties known to be susceptible to the fungal disease, and that no more than 25 percent of the acreage was planted to resistant varieties.
Krenzer estimated that the rust could cut yields by 10 to 15 percent on susceptible wheat varieties.
Mark Hodges, executive director of the Oklahoma Wheat Commission, gave a similar estimate when asked how much yields could suffer.
"I'd say five to 10 percent would be on the low side. Ten to 15 percent is more realistic," Hodges said. "At least half of the state's acreage will be affected with varying degrees of severity."
"The resistant varieties are holding up but the susceptible varieties -- we're going to have big problems with them," said Roger Gribble, northwest Oklahoma extension agronomist.
Hodges said Greer and Kiowa counties in southwest Oklahoma were among those areas worst-hit by the fungus.

In the most recent crop report, the U.S. Department of Agriculture said it expected Oklahoma to produce 125 million bushels of hard red winter wheat in 1997, which would be above actual 1996 production of 93.1 million bushels.
USDA said 6.8 million acres have been planted to wheat in Oklahoma, and the agency said it expected that 5.0 million of those acres would be harvested.
Oklahoma's Agricultural Statistics Service said Monday in its weekly crop progress report that disease problems appeared to concern many growers in the western part of the state.

The crop progress report rated the condition of the Oklahoma crop as 10 percent very poor, 17 percent poor, 39 fair, 33 good and one percent excellent. That marked a slight improvement over the previous week's rating of 14 percent very poor, 18 poor, 35 fair, 32 good and one excellent.
